title: Boss: the film quiz game
hook: Build a quiz game that asks, marks, scores and judges you.

warmup.explain: upper makes every letter a capital.
The 1 you give it is the starting number. Without it, it starts at 0.

warmup.q: What does `break` do inside a loop?
warmup.explain: break stops the loop and carries on with the lines after it.

why.heading: Boss day: a real game
why.text: Today you put the whole week together into one program. Nothing new to learn. You build a quiz in three steps. After each step you can run it and see it work. By task 3 it is a game you can give to someone else.

why.heading: Index cards in a stack
why.text:
A quiz is a stack of index cards. Each card has a question on one side and an answer on the other. In Python: a **list** is the stack, and each card is a **dictionary** with the keys `q` and `a`.

`{"q": "Tripod legs?", "a": "3"}`

why.heading: Grab a card's side
why.text: Loop through the stack: `for item in quiz:`. Each `item` is one card. Then `item["q"]` is its question and `item["a"]` is its answer. The question and answer data is long, so it is already typed for you in the starter.

why.heading: Fair marking
why.text: People type `SLATE` or ` slate `. So mark the answer after tidying it: `answer.lower().strip()`. Then compare it with `==` to the stored answer. Today's tools from earlier days all meet here: loops, input, if, dictionaries, text tools.

why.heading: The plan
why.text:
Step 1: print the questions, numbered.
Step 2: ask each question and say Correct or Nope.
Step 3: keep a score, then show the total and a final message that depends on how well you did.

watch.intro: Tap Run. A one-card quiz, to see the cards in action. The input is typed for you.
explain: `cards` is a list. Each card inside it is a dictionary with `q` and `a`.
`card['q']` is the question, used as the `input` prompt inside an f-string.
`answer.lower()` turns RED into red, so it matches.
Inside an f-string with double quotes, write the key with single quotes: `{card['q']}`. Otherwise the quotes clash.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: change `card["a"]` in the if line to `card["x"]` and tap Run. The error ends with `KeyError: 'x'`. The card has no key called x. Change it back.

tasks.title: Step 1: show the questions
tasks.task:
The quiz cards are ready. Loop through them and print each question numbered from 1:

`1. Cinema standard frames per second?`
`2. How many legs does a tripod have?`
`3. The board with the scene number?`
tasks.starter:
quiz = [
    {"q": "Cinema standard frames per second?", "a": "24"},
    {"q": "How many legs does a tripod have?", "a": "3"},
    {"q": "The board with the scene number?", "a": "slate"},
]
# loop and print the numbered questions
tasks.solution:
quiz = [
    {"q": "Cinema standard frames per second?", "a": "24"},
    {"q": "How many legs does a tripod have?", "a": "3"},
    {"q": "The board with the scene number?", "a": "slate"},
]
for n, item in enumerate(quiz, 1):
    print(f"{n}. {item['q']}")
hints: Numbers and items together means enumerate(quiz, 1).
for n, item in enumerate(quiz, 1): then an indented print.
print(f"{n}. {item['q']}") (single quotes around q inside the f-string)

tests.expect:
1. Cinema standard frames per second?
2. How many legs does a tripod have?
3. The board with the scene number?

tasks.title: Step 2: ask and mark
tasks.task:
Ask each question with `input`, using the question and a space as the prompt. Mark it: if the answer (lower case, spaces stripped) matches the card, print `Correct!`, otherwise print `Nope:` and the right answer. Example, answering all three:

`Cinema standard frames per second? 24`
`Correct!`
`How many legs does a tripod have? 3`
`Correct!`
`The board with the scene number? slate`
`Correct!`
tasks.starter:
quiz = [
    {"q": "Cinema standard frames per second?", "a": "24"},
    {"q": "How many legs does a tripod have?", "a": "3"},
    {"q": "The board with the scene number?", "a": "slate"},
]
# loop, ask, mark

tests.expect:
Cinema standard frames per second? 24
Correct!
How many legs does a tripod have? 3
Correct!
The board with the scene number? slate
Correct!

Cinema standard frames per second? 25
Nope: 24
How many legs does a tripod have? 3
Correct!
The board with the scene number? SLATE
Correct!

tasks.title: Step 3: score and verdict
tasks.task: The marking loop is done. Add a `score` that goes up by 1 for each correct answer. After the loop print `Score: 2 out of 3` (with the real numbers), then one final message: all correct prints `Perfect! Frame it.`, at least one correct prints `Good effort. Run it again.`, none correct prints `Back to film school!`
hints: Set score = 0 before the loop, and score += 1 inside the Correct branch.
After the loop use len(quiz) for the total: print(f"Score: {score} out of {len(quiz)}")
Then if score == len(quiz): ... elif score >= 1: ... else: ... with a print in each.

recap: A list of dictionaries is a stack of index cards: loop the list, look up the keys.
Tidy the player's answer with `.lower().strip()` before you compare.
A score is a counter: start at 0, `+= 1` for each win.
You built a whole game from week 1 to 3 tools. Change the cards and it becomes any quiz you like.

words.meaning: A list where every item is a dictionary, like a stack of cards.
A number that goes up when you win a point.
Use == to check if two things are the same.
A day where you combine earlier ideas into one finished thing.
